argument: The chapter's whole case is that a weapon is identity rather than a stat line, so its own table should never rank two arms against each other. The ranged rows do exactly that, and the prose says the opposite: every weapon hits identically, pick on feel, not on paper strength. Shortbow and longbow share a discipline cell, an empty property cell and the 60/120 ft range, yet the longbow asks double the gold. The crossbow, at the shortbow's exact 25 gp, adds a reload Maneuver and drops to 20/60 ft. Paying equal or more therefore buys no column back, so two entries are strictly dominated, which the locked flavour law bans at matching price. A table that ranks its own rows falsifies the promise the chapter makes in prose, and the flavour law it claims to satisfy.

evidence.claim: The shortbow row carries one Archery discipline, an empty properties cell and a 60/120 ft range at 25 gp.
The longbow row repeats the identical discipline, empty properties cell and 60/120 ft range but charges 50 gp, so nothing in the table pays for the doubling.
The crossbow sits at the shortbow's own 25 gp while adding the Loading handicap and halving range to 20/60 ft, giving no compensating column.
The prose instructs the reader that all weapons hit for the same numbers and should be chosen on feel rather than table strength, which the cost and range columns contradict.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: They all hit the same; you are the one doing the hitting

evidence.claim: The locked weapon-as-flavour law forbids any weapon being strictly better than another at the same price, which the shortbow does to the crossbow at 25 gp.
evidence.quote_or_excerpt: No weapon may be strictly better than another at the same cost
